results.claim: The problem has an exact objective-preserving Local Neighborhood Test Cover reformulation: after adjoining a dummy element, admissible tests are nonempty subsets of a host's closed neighborhood, and every pair of elements must be separated. Approximation and inapproximability results transfer in both directions without loss.
results.proof_sketch: For G=(V,E), adjoin a dummy element ⊥. A local test is a pair (z,M) with z∈V and ∅≠M⊆N[z]; ⊥ belongs to no test. A family covers the test instance when every unordered pair in V∪{⊥} is separated by some M. Given a surveillance system, replace each bug b hosted at z_b by (z_b,M(b)) and set S(⊥)=∅. Test M(b) separates x and y exactly when b belongs to precisely one of S(x),S(y). Thus separation of each pair {v,⊥} is equivalent to S(v)≠∅, while separation of each pair {u,v} is equivalent to S(u)≠S(v). Conversely, host one bug at z for every test (z,M) and tune it to M; the same equivalences give legal nonempty pairwise-distinct signatures. Empty-zone or duplicate tests are unnecessary and may be deleted. Both transformations preserve the number of objects and have polynomial certificate size, so OPT and every approximation ratio coincide, and hardness transfers identically.

results.claim: Fixed-placement feasibility has an exact matching characterization, yielding an XP exact algorithm parameterized by the number k of bugs.
results.proof_sketch: Fix a multiset B of bugs and their host intervals. For each safe house v, let A(v) be the bugs hosted in N[v]. Construct a bipartite graph whose left side is the safe houses and whose right side consists of all nonempty subsets of B; join v to S exactly when S⊆A(v). A matching saturating all safe houses is precisely an assignment of distinct nonempty feasible signatures. Conversely, such signatures define each bug's monitored set. Thus one can test a placement by bipartite matching, or by the source's polynomial lexicographic test. Enumerating the binomial(n+k−1,k) multisets of k host locations gives an n^{k+O(1)} exact decision algorithm for OPT≤k.

results.claim: Regional information bound: for every X⊆V, at least ceil(log2(|X|+1)) bugs must be hosted in N[X]. Moreover, the optimum is additive over connected components.
results.proof_sketch: Every signature of a vertex in X uses only bugs whose hosts lie in N[X]=union_{x∈X}N[x]. If h bugs are hosted there, only 2^h−1 nonempty subsets of those bugs exist, so |X|≤2^h−1. If several sets X_i have pairwise disjoint N[X_i], their bounds add. For components, no bug can hear across components, so restricting any solution to each component gives a solution there. Conversely, componentwise solutions can be united: their bug sets are disjoint, and nonempty signatures from different components therefore cannot coincide. Hence OPT(G)=sum_C OPT(C).

results.claim: If every connected component C has a universal safe house, then OPT is exactly sum_C ceil(log2(|C|+1)), computable in polynomial time.
results.proof_sketch: The information bound applied to a component C gives OPT(C)≥ceil(log2(|C|+1)). If u is universal in C, put that many bugs at u. Every safe house can hear all of them, so assign the |C| houses arbitrary distinct nonempty subsets. This attains the lower bound. Component additivity proves the formula. Components and universal vertices can be found in polynomial time.

results.claim: Incidence-capacity lower bound: if rho=max_v |N[v]| and a solution has k bugs, then L(n,k)≤k rho, where L(n,k) is the minimum total cardinality of n distinct nonempty subsets of a k-element set.
results.proof_sketch: Let the signatures be S(v). Double-count incidences: sum_v |S(v)|=sum_b |M(b)|. A bug hosted at z monitors only a subset of N[z], so the right side is at most k rho. The left side is minimized by taking subsets in increasing cardinality. Explicitly, if s is least with sum_{j=1}^s binomial(k,j)≥n, then L(n,k)=sum_{j=1}^{s−1} j binomial(k,j)+s(n−sum_{j=1}^{s−1}binomial(k,j)). In particular, at most k signatures are singletons, so L(n,k)≥2n−k.

results.claim: The problem is exactly solvable on interval graphs of maximum degree at most two. For every connected component C of order n, OPT(C)=floor(n/2)+1; componentwise summation gives the general answer.
results.proof_sketch: A connected maximum-degree-two graph is a path or cycle. An interval graph has no induced cycle of length at least four: for a cycle interval with minimum right endpoint, both cycle neighbors contain that endpoint and hence intersect, creating a chord. Thus only paths and K3 occur, and OPT(K3)=2. For P_n, 2n−k≤sum_v|S(v)|≤3k, so k≥ceil(n/2). If n=2t and k=t, equality forces every bug to monitor a complete three-vertex neighborhood, all t singleton codes to occur, and every other code to be a pair. Cohosted bugs have identical monitored neighborhoods and therefore cannot have singleton codes. Bugs at adjacent hosts make both host vertices contain their two bugs; since those codes have size two, they coincide. Hence the t hosts would have to be distinct nonadjacent internal vertices, but P_{2t} has at most t−1 such positions. Thus k≥t+1. Bugs on all odd vertices attain the formula for odd paths; for even paths, add a bug at the last vertex and use singleton codes on hosts and adjacent pairs between them.

results.claim: Running the source greedy algorithm in both timeline directions and taking the better result is not exact, even on a connected symmetric instance: both runs use seven bugs while OPT=6.
results.proof_sketch: Take L1=[−2/5,0], L2=[−2/5,1], L3=[3/5,2], L4=[8/5,3], L5=[8/5,4], L6=[13/5,5], U=[7/2,23/2], and let Ri be the reflection of Li under x↦15−x. Exact execution adds bugs at processing/host positions (1,2),(2,3),(4,6),(6,7),(9,11),(11,13),(13,13), totaling seven; reflection gives the same trace in the opposite direction. Six bugs suffice: host a,b,c at L2,L3,L5 and d,e,f at R5,R3,R2. Give L1,…,L6 codes {a},{a,b},{a,b,c},{b},{b,c},{c}; give R1,…,R6 codes {f},{e,f},{d,e,f},{e},{d,e},{d}; and give U code {c,d}. These codes are legal, nonempty, and distinct. The four leftmost L-vertices have neighborhood exactly the six L-vertices and therefore require three bugs hosted there. The symmetric right region independently requires three bugs in its disjoint six-vertex neighborhood. Hence OPT≥6, proving OPT=6.

results.claim: There is a connected ten-interval instance on which the source greedy algorithm uses five bugs in each timeline direction while OPT=4; thus the bidirectional variant has approximation ratio at least 5/4.
results.proof_sketch:
In timeline order take I1=[0,3], I2=[1,5], I3=[2,6], I4=[9,10], I5=[4,11], I6=[7,12], I7=[14,16], I8=[15,17], I9=[8,18], I10=[13,19]. The graph is connected. Four bugs suffice: host a at I2, b at I5, and c,d at I9, and assign codes ({a},{a,b},{b},{b,c,d},{a,c},{b,d},{c,d},{d},{b,c},{c}) to I1,…,I10. They are legal and pairwise distinct. Since ten nonempty distinct signatures cannot be formed from three bugs, OPT≥ceil(log2(11))=4.

For the forward run, feasibility before steps 1,…,10 is F,F,T,F,T,T,F,T,T,F, giving additions (processing position,host position) (1,3),(2,5),(4,9),(7,10),(10,10). At the five F steps, Hall-deficient vertex sets are {1}, {1,2}, {1,2,3,4}, {1,2,3,4,6,7}, and {1,2,3,4,6,7,8,10}; their unions of available nonzero signatures have sizes 0,1,3,5,7, respectively. At the T steps, binary-mask matching certificates in prefix order are (1,3,2), (1,3,2,6,4), (1,3,2,6,5,4), (1,3,2,6,5,4,12,8), and (1,3,2,6,5,4,12,8,10). Masks use the current bugs as low-to-high bits.

The reverse order is I8,I7,I10,I4,I9,I6,I5,I3,I2,I1. Its pattern is F,F,T,F,T,T,T,F,T,F, with additions (1,5),(2,5),(4,7),(8,10),(10,10). Using the whole current prefix, Hall deficits at the F steps are 1>0, 2>1, 4>3, 8>7, and 10>9; matching masks at the T steps are (3,2,1), (3,2,1,5,4), (3,2,1,6,5,4), (3,2,1,7,6,5,4), and (3,2,1,7,6,5,4,12,8). Thus both runs use five.

results.claim: For every t≥1 there is an interval instance with OPT=4t on which both timeline directions use 5t bugs; consequently 5/4 is an asymptotic lower bound for the bidirectional greedy approximation ratio.
results.proof_sketch: Take t translated copies of the ten-interval instance, separated far enough that distinct copies do not intersect. Component additivity gives OPT=4t. In the forward timeline, the copies occur consecutively and each induces the same forward execution. Bugs placed in earlier components are unavailable in the current component, while every nonempty signature in the current component uses its new, disjoint bug identities and therefore cannot equal a signature from an earlier component. Hence the feasibility decisions and five additions repeat independently in every copy, for 5t bugs. Reflecting the entire family reverses the copy order and induces the certified reverse execution within each copy, again producing 5t bugs. Taking the better direction still returns 5t, so its cost divided by OPT is exactly 5/4 for arbitrarily large instances.

final_writeup:
The general target remains unresolved. This revision does not give a polynomial-time approximation ratio strictly below 2 for arbitrary interval families and does not prove a matching inapproximability theorem. It does, however, add an exact target-equivalent structural reformulation while preserving the asymptotic 5/4 obstruction for the natural bidirectional version of the source algorithm.

Model the instance by its interval graph G. A bug hosted at z can be tuned to any subset of N[z]. Every vertex v must receive a nonempty signature S(v), and these signatures must be pairwise distinct.

Adjoin a dummy element ⊥ having the empty signature. Regard every bug hosted at z with monitored set M as a local test (z,M), where ∅≠M⊆N[z]. Such a test separates two elements exactly when it contains one of them. The surveillance conditions say precisely that every pair in V∪{⊥} is separated: pairs {v,⊥} enforce nonempty vertex signatures, and pairs {u,v} enforce distinct signatures. Conversely, any family of these local tests becomes a surveillance system by hosting and tuning the corresponding bugs. This preserves solution size exactly. Thus the open approximation-or-hardness target is equivalently the same target for this implicitly represented Local Neighborhood Test Cover problem. The reformulation alone supplies neither side of that dichotomy.

For fixed bug placements, feasibility is exactly a saturating-matching question. Let A(v) be the bugs hosted in N[v], and join v to every nonempty subset of A(v). A matching saturating V assigns precisely the required legal distinct signatures; conversely, any surveillance system supplies such a matching. Enumerating all host multisets of size at most k gives an n^{k+O(1)} XP exact algorithm for OPT≤k.

The verified lower bounds remain useful. For every X⊆V, all bugs heard by X are hosted in N[X], so at least ceil(log2(|X|+1)) bugs must be hosted there. Bounds from sets with disjoint neighborhood unions add, and OPT is exactly additive over connected components. Also, if rho=max_v|N[v]|, double-counting bug-signature incidences gives L(n,k)≤k rho for every k-bug solution, where L(n,k) is the least total size of n distinct nonempty k-bit signatures.

These bounds are exact on useful boundary classes. A component with a universal safe house has optimum ceil(log2(|C|+1)). A maximum-degree-two interval component is a path or K3, and its optimum is floor(|C|/2)+1; the even-path lower bound requires the equality-case obstruction that t hosts cannot be distinct nonadjacent internal vertices of P_{2t}.

The connected reflection-symmetric example remains valid: both directions use seven bugs while two disjoint regional bounds and an explicit code system prove OPT=6.

The stronger obstruction uses the ten timeline-ordered intervals

I1=[0,3], I2=[1,5], I3=[2,6], I4=[9,10], I5=[4,11], I6=[7,12], I7=[14,16], I8=[15,17], I9=[8,18], I10=[13,19].

They induce a connected interval graph. Host bugs a at I2, b at I5, and c,d at I9. The codes

{a}, {a,b}, {b}, {b,c,d}, {a,c}, {b,d}, {c,d}, {d}, {b,c}, {c}

for I1,…,I10 are legal, nonempty, and distinct. Thus OPT≤4, while 2^3−1<10 gives OPT≥4.

In the forward direction the source rule adds at processing/host positions (1,3),(2,5),(4,9),(7,10),(10,10). In the reflected direction, whose order is I8,I7,I10,I4,I9,I6,I5,I3,I2,I1, it adds at (1,5),(2,5),(4,7),(8,10),(10,10). Exact Hall-deficit certificates establish every infeasible prefix, and explicit saturating matchings establish every intervening feasible prefix. Hence each run uses five bugs and the better run has ratio 5/4.

Taking arbitrarily many mutually disjoint translated copies preserves the five additions per copy in either direction: bugs cannot be heard across components, and nonempty signatures over disjoint bug identities cannot collide. Component additivity gives OPT=4t and bidirectional cost 5t. Therefore no analysis can give this bidirectional heuristic a guarantee strictly below 5/4.
